newsitem.title: USA: Senators say Army sex cases show separation needed.
newsitem.headline: Senators say Army sex cases show separation needed.

text.p: The Army said on Tuesday it was investigating 1,074 allegations of sexual harassment including rape, prompting several senators to challenge the training of female recruits with men under male sergeants.

Army Chief of Staff Gen. Dennis Reimer told the Senate Armed Services Committee 20 percent of the allegations are of rape or harassment in the past two years and 33 percent involve incidents ten years ago or more.

Reimer and other Army officials provided no new details on charges of rape or sexual harassment against seven drill instructors at the nearby Aberdeen Proving Ground or sex harassment investigations of 48 men there and at the Fort Leonard Wood training centre in Missouri.

While the Senate hearing was in progress, Aberdeen officials announced that charges of rape, sodomy and other abuse of female recruits had been filed against a seventh soldier there, Staff Sgt. Vernell Robinson.

Reimer and Army Secretary Togo West had no substantive comment on a new allegation that Sgt. Maj. of the Army Gene McKinney had been accused by a female sergeant of sexually attacking her in a Hawaii hotel last year.
McKinney, the Army's top sergeant, denied the charge and Army officials at the Pentagon said he will remain on duty there while the charges against him are investigated.
Several senators said the high sex harassment numbers show the Army is holding a match near a powder keg by having women recruits train with men under male drill instructors.
"Sexuality is one of the most basic of all human instincts," Sen. Dan Coats, an Indiana Republican, said. He asked later : "Do we have our heads in the sand?"

West said he was shocked at the leaders' abuse of their power over subordinates and said the issue was not one of whether trainees have consentual sex with each other in barracks. But Coats told West he was surprised at his shock.

"To say that someone's shocked over the fact that somebody has absolute authority over a young female (and you have) incidents like these ... ignores basic fundamental understanding of human behaviour," Coats said.
"Senator, that says less about our non-commissioned officers (sergeants) than we think of them," West responded.

Reimer said the Army trains men and women together because they are going to have to work together. He said he was confident the Army can continue the mixed training and get rid of what he called "a few bad apples" who abuse their power.
Sen. Pat Roberts, a Kansas Republican, suggested men and women recruits be trained separately to avoid the male drill sergeant abuses and then work together later.

But Sen. Joseph Lieberman, a Connecticut Democrat, said segregated training would punish women twice: failing to protect them against sexual abuse and then lessening their ability to serve effectively in the Army.
